pedagogy.summary: This extends line plots to eighth-inch precision and, crucially, USES the plotted data for computation — finding the difference between the longest and shortest specimen, or totalling all the measurements — which requires adding and subtracting fractions with like and related denominators. Two skills are fused: build an accurate 1/8 scale, and operate on the fractions read from it. It is best taught by generating data, plotting to the nearest 1/8, then posing genuine questions answerable only from the plot (difference, total, redistribution), with the eighth scale showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½) so common denominators are visible on the axis itself.
bestPractices: Measure to the nearest 1/8 inch with a subdivided ruler and scale the axis into equal eighths
Make equivalence visible on the scale — mark that 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½ — so common denominators for later arithmetic are seen, not just computed
Pose real difference and total problems that can only be answered by reading positions and adding fractions
Stress that a stack of Xs contributes its value once per X (three Xs at 3/8 add 3/8 three times) — multiplicity matters when totalling
Keep the one-X-per-case rule and connect eighths back to quarters and halves
keyRepresentations: A number line in eighths showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½)
Fraction bars for adding and subtracting like denominators
The plot itself used as a data source for computation
commonMisconceptions: When asked for a total length, adding or counting the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
Adding fractions by adding numerators AND denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
Spacing eighths unequally or not seeing 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
Counting a value only once when several Xs are stacked on it while totalling

learn.summary: Grade 4 measurement line plots at eighth-inch precision, fused with using the plotted data for fraction arithmetic. Learners measure specimens to the nearest 1/8 inch, build an equal-interval eighth scale, plot one X per object, then answer genuine questions that require adding and subtracting fractions with like/related denominators: the difference between longest and shortest, and the total length of everything. The key insight comes when totalling over stacks: three Xs at 3/8 contribute 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so frequency (how many Xs) and value (how much length) diverge. Marking 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2 on the axis makes common denominators visible, so 1/2 − 3/8 becomes 4/8 − 3/8 right on the scale.

activities.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
feedback: If the learner gives the number of objects as the 'total', point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?', holding 'how many objects' apart from 'how much length'.
If the learner adds each distinct axis value only once while ignoring stack height, show that each X on the stack contributes its value again (three Xs at 3/8 give 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
If the learner writes 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16, reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts: the denominator (the size of the part) stays the same, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
If ticks are mis-spaced or 1/2 − 3/8 is attempted without a common denominator, overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale and use a fraction strip to find the common denominator (1/2 = 4/8).
activities.rationale: The standard asks learners both to make a line plot in fractions of a unit and to solve addition/subtraction problems using that plot, so building and computing should be fused rather than separated. Posing a total over stacked Xs directly targets the documented frequency-vs-value confusion.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
learnerActions: Measure several real objects (e.g. seedlings or paper strips) to the nearest 1/8 inch using a ruler subdivided into eighths; include some objects that share a length.
Draw a number line marked in equally spaced intervals that each represent 1/8 inch, and plot one X per object at its measured value.
Mark where 2/8 lines up with 1/4 and where 4/8 lines up with 1/2 directly on the axis.
Find longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions, converting to a common denominator on the scale (e.g. 1/2 − 3/8 = 4/8 − 3/8 = 1/8).
Find the total length of all objects by adding each object's value with multiplicity — a stack of three Xs at 3/8 contributes 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, not '3'.
Predict how the total changes if one more object at 1/2 is added, then check (the total rises by 1/2 = 4/8).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate eighth scale makes equivalences (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2) and common denominators visible, and totalling over a plot means summing measured values with multiplicity — which is different from counting Xs.

activities.title: Compute from a given plot: difference and total
feedback: If the answer equals the count of Xs, revisit the distinction between how many Xs and how much length.
If a non-standard sum appears (e.g. denominators added, giving 6/16), reteach that same-size parts are joined with the denominator unchanged, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
Confirm correct work by checking the common-denominator conversion against the axis ticks (e.g. 1/2 reads as 4/8).
activities.rationale: When the plot is given, the operate-on-data half of the skill — solving addition and subtraction of fraction problems from line-plot data — can be exercised in a focused, checkable way. This is a scaffold that isolates computation; it does not exercise constructing the scale or measuring to the nearest 1/8.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
learnerActions: From a pre-drawn eighth-scale plot, state the longest and shortest values and compute longest − shortest over a common denominator.
Compute the total length, taking care that a stack of several Xs at one value contributes that value once per X.
Choose which of several candidate totals is correct, and explain why the count of Xs is NOT the total length.
activities.intendedInsight: Given an accurate plot, the difference and total are determined by reading positions and adding/subtracting fractions correctly, keeping multiplicity in mind.

activities.title: Reveal equivalence on the eighth scale (reference scaffold)
feedback: Confirm when the learner names an equivalence correctly; prompt 'what else is this the same as?' to surface 2/8 = 1/4.
If a stack's total is read as the number of Xs, reveal the repeated-value sum to contrast count with length.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference can make equivalence and stack contribution concrete and label positions, supporting the fuller build-and-compute work. As a reference it does not exercise measuring to the nearest 1/8 or performing the computations independently, so it supports rather than replaces the main activity.
learnerActions: Tap or point to a position on an eighth-scale line and read off its equivalent (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2).
Tap a stack of Xs to reveal its combined contribution to the total (e.g. three Xs at 3/8 reveal 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
Name where 1/4 and 1/2 sit and what else each is the same as.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same point on an eighth scale, and a stack's contribution is its value repeated once per X.

constraints: Learners must construct the scale themselves and measure to the nearest 1/8 inch; a given-plot or tap-to-reveal task isolates computation or shows equivalence but does not exercise building an accurate eighth scale or measuring.
Scale-building should be assessed through actual construction; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of an equal-interval scale.
Keep the one-X-per-case convention, and ensure eighth intervals are drawn equally spaced so quarter/half ticks line up.
The total must be computed by summing measured values with multiplicity, not by counting Xs; keep frequency and value explicitly distinct.

Adding fractions that have the same denominator keeps the denominator unchanged (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8); adding denominators (giving 6/16) is an error. When denominators are related but different (e.g. 1/2 and 3/8), first rewrite them with a common denominator (1/2 = 4/8) before adding or subtracting.

An interactive panel showing live arithmetic (e.g. selecting a stack to lay out 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8) or overlaying quarter/half ticks is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required tool; the same reasoning can be done with a ruler, drawn number line and fraction strips.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that a static image and a scale-blind quiz 'cannot' build the fusion of multiplicity and fraction addition, and that a spatial dimension or dialogue 'adds nothing'. These are catalogue-fit judgements, not established necessity claims; here they are softened to scoped affordances/limits (given-plot tasks isolate computation; tap-to-reveal is a reference).

The cited standard (4.MD.B.4) supports making the plot and solving add/subtract problems from it, but does not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interactive or reference format; no efficacy claim is made, which is why the reference activity carries no sourceClaims.

The Kaplan et al. source documents persistent frequency-vs-value confusion in histograms/dot plots; its transfer to line-plot totalling is plausible and used to justify the total-over-stacks probe, but the source does not test this specific activity.
'Redistribution' appears in the source pedagogy as a third question type but is not separately operationalised here; difference and total are the operationalised computations.

Fresh independent review: fraction arithmetic (1/2 − 3/8 = 1/8; three at 3/8 = 9/8; +1/2 = +4/8; 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8) verified; no categorical medium-superiority claims remain in summary, insights, actions, feedback or constraints.

probeDeeper: You have three Xs at 3/8 — how much length is that altogether, and why isn't it just 3?
To find longest minus shortest you need ½ take away 3/8 — how do you make those two comparable?
Where is ¼ on your eighth scale? What else is it the same as?
If I added one more object at ½, how would the total change?
assess.correctAnswer: Builds an equal-interval eighth-inch scale, plots one X per object, finds longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions over a common denominator, and totals by adding each object's value WITH multiplicity (a stack of three at 3/8 contributes 3/8 three times), recognising 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½.

errorPatterns.pattern: When asked for total length, adds or counts the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?'; hold apart 'how many objects' from 'how much length'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the number of objects as the 'total', or adds each distinct axis value once while ignoring stack height

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by adding numerators and denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts using fraction bars, denominator unchanged
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Non-standard sums when totalling or differencing the measurements

errorPatterns.pattern: Spaces eighths unequally or doesn't see 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale to show equivalence; use a fraction strip to find the common denominator
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mis-spaced ticks, or subtracting ½ − 3/8 without converting to a common denominator

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build an accurate eighth scale or cannot operate on the fractions; totals by counting Xs or adds denominators.
responseLevels.full: Builds an equal-interval eighth scale showing equivalence, plots one X per case, and computes both difference and total correctly — summing values with multiplicity and using common denominators — transferring to an added data point.
responseLevels.partial: Builds and reads the plot and can do one operation (e.g. the difference) but mishandles multiplicity in totals or needs prompting to find a common denominator; lists values without combining them correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler marked in eighths and several objects, some sharing a length. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest eighth inch, plot them, then tell me the difference between the longest and shortest, and the total length of all of them.' Watch the scale-building, and especially watch how they handle stacks of more than one X when totalling, and how they subtract the two fractional positions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for a TOTAL over stacks forces the child to separate frequency (count of Xs) from value (length) AND to add fractions correctly. A child running the bar-graph habit totals by counting Xs; a child adding numerators and denominators produces a specific wrong sum. Each error shows a different, diagnosable signature in both the plot and the arithmetic — which asking about the procedure would not reveal.
